title: What Is Inflation?
paragraphs: Inflation tends to make itself felt in everyday life well before it appears in the headlines: grocery bills creep up, rents rise and a fixed income seems to buy a little less each month. Economists define it as a sustained increase in the general price level, and since it shapes the purchasing power of every household and firm, it ranks among the most scrutinised indicators of economic health.

At its core, inflation erodes the real value of money. Where nominal wages stagnate while prices climb, living standards fall, and cash savings steadily lose value. To quantify the process, national statistics agencies compile a consumer price index, which tracks the cost of a representative basket of goods and services, encompassing food, energy, housing and transport, and compares it with the corresponding figure twelve months earlier.

The causes are usually grouped into two broad categories. Demand-pull inflation arises when aggregate spending outstrips the economy's productive capacity, enabling sellers to raise prices. Cost-push inflation originates on the supply side, as sharp increases in the cost of energy, raw materials or labour are passed on to consumers. A rapid expansion of the money supply can amplify either form.

Responsibility for price stability typically lies with an independent central bank, many of which pursue an inflation target of roughly two percent a year. The principal lever at their disposal is the policy interest rate: raising it increases the cost of borrowing and rewards saving, thereby dampening demand. Its effects, however, materialise only gradually, often taking many months to filter through to consumer prices.
